sections.heading: The one test: must it be true?
sections.body:
Logic questions give you some **statements**, also called **premises**. A premise is a fact you must accept as true, even if it sounds odd. You then pick the **conclusion**, the statement that **must** follow from them.

A conclusion must be true only if there is **no way** to keep every premise true and make the conclusion false.

To test a choice, look for a **counterexample**: a small made-up situation where every premise is true but the choice is false. If you can build one, the choice is wrong.

Use only the statements given. Real-life knowledge does not count.

sections.heading: All, some and no: draw circles
sections.body:
A **syllogism** is a set of "all", "some" or "no" statements followed by a conclusion. Picture each group as a circle:

| Statement | Circle sketch |
| --- | --- |
| All A are B | The A circle sits **inside** the B circle |
| No A are B | The two circles **do not touch** |
| Some A are B | The circles **overlap**, with at least one person in the overlap |
| Some A are not B | At least one A is **outside** the B circle |

**"Some" means "at least one"**, and it could even be all of them.

**Example.** All nurses are health workers. All health workers are vaccinated. The nurses circle sits inside health workers, which sits inside vaccinated, so **all nurses are vaccinated**. But "all vaccinated people are nurses" does not follow: a vaccinated farmer keeps both premises true.

For a "some" statement, give the person in the overlap a name and follow that person through the other statements.

sections.heading: If-then statements
sections.body:
A **conditional** is an if-then statement: "if p, then q". p is the **if-part** and q is the **then-part**.

Rule: If the power goes out, the elevator stops.

| You know | You conclude | Valid? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The power goes out | The elevator stops | **Yes** (modus ponens) |
| The elevator did not stop | The power did not go out | **Yes** (contrapositive) |
| The elevator stopped | The power went out | **No** (affirming the consequent) |
| The power did not go out | The elevator did not stop | **No** (denying the antecedent) |

**Modus ponens** means moving forward: the if-part happened, so the then-part happens. The last two rows fail because the elevator could stop for another reason, like repairs.

The **contrapositive**, "if not q, then not p", always means the same as the rule. The **converse**, "if q, then p", does not.

sections.heading: And, or, not
sections.body:
A **connective** is a word that joins small statements into a **compound statement**. Logic writes them as symbols; the exam uses words.

| Words | Symbol | The compound is true when... |
| --- | --- | --- |
| not p | ¬p | p is false |
| p and q | p ∧ q | both parts are true |
| p or q | p ∨ q | at least one part is true (both is fine) |
| if p, then q | p → q | every case except p true and q false |

**Method:** mark each small part T (true) or F (false), then combine.

**Example.** The jeep is full (T). It is raining (F). "The jeep is full or it is raining" is T or F: **true**. "The jeep is full and it is raining" is T and F: **false**.

To deny an "and": "not (p and q)" means "not p, **or** not q".

sections.heading: Ordering and seating
sections.body:
1. Rewrite every clue with one word. "Nestor is younger than Mara" becomes "Mara is older than Nestor".
2. Draw a line (oldest to youngest) or numbered seats. Place the clues that give an exact spot first.
3. If a clue allows two options, such as "sits at one end", work out **each case**.
4. The answer must be true in **every** case. Two people the clues never compare can be in either order.

**Example.** Lino is older than Mara. Nestor is younger than Mara. Line: Lino, Mara, Nestor. So Lino is older than Nestor.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.body:
- **Turning "all" around.** All clerks are employees does not mean all employees are clerks.
- **Reading "some are" as "some are not".** "Some drivers sing" does not mean some drivers don't.
- **A shared middle group.** All A are B and some B are C: the C's may all be outside A.
- **Swapping the order in "some ... are not".** Some A are not B is a different claim from some B are not A.
- **Going backward on an if-then.** A stopped elevator does not prove the power went out.
- **A false if-part.** When the if-part is false, the rule tells you nothing about the then-part.
- **"Or" as "one but not both".** In logic, "p or q" is still true when both parts are true.
- **"Could be" is not "must be".** Always try for a counterexample.

glossaryTerms.definition: A statement you are given and must accept as true when you reason.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Premise – ibinigay na pahayag na tatanggapin mong totoo, kahit kakaiba pakinggan

glossaryTerms.definition: A statement that is claimed to follow from the premises.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Conclusion – ang hinuha o resulta na dapat lumabas mula sa mga premise

glossaryTerms.definition: A situation where all the premises are true but a choice is false. It proves the choice does not have to be true.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Counterexample – halimbawang sitwasyon na totoo lahat ng premise pero mali ang choice, kaya hindi ito "must be true"

glossaryTerms.definition: A set of "all", "some" or "no" statements followed by a conclusion.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Syllogism – mga pahayag na may "all", "some" o "no" na sinusundan ng conclusion; i-drawing bilang mga bilog

glossaryTerms.definition: An if-then statement: "if p, then q". It promises that whenever p happens, q happens.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Conditional – pahayag na "kung p, then q"; tuwing mangyari ang p, mangyayari ang q

glossaryTerms.definition: "If not q, then not p". It always means the same as "if p, then q".
glossaryTerms.taglish: Contrapositive – baligtarin ang dalawang bahagi at lagyan pareho ng "not"; pareho pa rin ang ibig sabihin

glossaryTerms.definition: "If q, then p". It swaps the parts and does not mean the same as the original rule.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Converse – pinagpalit lang ang dalawang bahagi; iba na ang ibig sabihin, kaya bitag ito

glossaryTerms.definition: A word such as "and", "or", "not" or "if-then" that joins small statements into a compound statement.
glossaryTerms.taglish: Connective – salitang nagdudugtong ng mga pahayag, gaya ng "and", "or", "not"
